articles.headline: INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.
articles.text:
INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.

We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views, representing the most interesting events of the range cattle industry. There are thirty-six well-executed photographs in the series, making an extremely interesting and realistic panorama of cowboy life. We will sell the complete set for $5 or,

THE COW BOY A YEAR AND THE SET, $6

This offer will probably be recalled soon, but the bargain can now be secured by calling on or addressing THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy offers Huffman's set of thirty-six round-up photographs for $5, or $6 with a year's subscription.

articles.text: The report comes from Bismarck, that Supt. Green, in his candidacy for the legislature, has been up and down the road in his private car, telling all the railroad men that they must vote for him. We are no champion of Mr. Green's, but we do not believe in this way of fighting the candidate of an opposition party. While here, Mr. Green told several railroad men that they ought to vote as they thought best and that no pressure of any kind would be brought to bear on them. This was not said publicly or for effect, but personally to different railroad men.

articles.text: At the coming session of the legislature, a bill will be introduced from Billings county for a rebate of the railroad taxes paid into the territorial treasury on account of its mileage in Billings county while it was yet unorganized. The Cow Boy has several times mentioned this matter and a full discussion only shows the more plainly that we should receive the back taxes. We see no difference in our relations, while unorganized, to the territory than there is between a ward and a guardian. The taxes are simply held in trust for us by the Territory until we reach our majority by organization. This we have done and now of course we want a settlment from our guardian. The amount involved is about $10,000; enough to pay our county expenses for two or three years.

articles.text: A New York syndicate now has agents in the field who are negotiating for the purchase of the whole Cherokee strip. articles.text: There is no question that the present pool rate established on both live and dressed beef between Chicago and New York is exorbitant and will call for general discussion at all the meetings of the cattle associations. In spite of the fact that beef is selling lower than for several years, these roads have increased the freight rate to a higher point than it has ever been since there was any competition. This of course, affects stockmen directly, as it costs from $1 to $1.25 more to market a steer than it has hitherto. This applies whether the animal is sold in Chicago or New York. In short, should the present rate continue, stockmen can figure that they will lose at least a dollar a head on all their beef cattle. This matter is worth looking into and remedy ing.
articles.summary: There is no question that the present pool rate established on both live and dressed beef between Chicago and New York is exorbitant and will call for general discussion at all the meetings of the cattle associations.

articles.text: The fact that it pays to feed cattle is abundantly demonstrated in the case of the Powder River cattle company. For several years they have been running large feeding pens near Duluth and they state that it nets them from $10 to $12 on every animal they have fed. This makes a splendid margin and applies to all classes of cattle not in the very best condition. The feed consists principally of wheat screenings, ground and boiled. Oat straw and prairie hay are also fed. The animals are tied in rows in large barns and are seldom liberated before being sent to market. When a shipment arrives, the animals are tied up as rapidly as possible, for they get exceedingly wild if allowed to stand in the yard more than a day or two. After the second day in the stable, they eat ravenously and often get as gentle as barnyard cows. When liberated, however, they become as wild as ever. This company has now fed so long and with such unifom success that it has entirely passed the experimental stage. There are occasionally animals that do not fatten well but they are only the exceptions that prove the rule; they have averaged over $10 a head on all the animals they have ever fattened, the feeding extending over a period of several years. We expect to see the example of the Powder River cattle Co. largely followed by range stockmen. There is no reason why it should not be a success for all, as well as one.
articles.summary: The fact that it pays to feed cattle is abundantly demonstrated in the case of the Powder River cattle company.

articles.text: There is no business on the face of the earth which depends so entiely on providence and honest neighbors as the cattle business. There is no business that covers such an area for every operator and none in which there are so many chances for leaks to foot up large totals. In spite of these facts, there is no class of men who place such implicit reliance in final results and certainly no class of men, taken as a class and not individual who are so utterly careless of their vital interests as are cowmen. Time after time, important measures need to be adopted and fail, either from lack of unanimity or because the most of the stockmen are too careless or lazy to look after their own interests. There is no need in specifying particular instances. A score will come to the mind of any one in the range country. Now however, the most vital question touching the stock interests is the threatened spread of pleuro-pneumonia. The stockmen should rise as one man and demand that not alone should every diseased animal be killed in the United States, but that hereafter and forevermore, not a solitary animal should be imported from any country not absolutely free from the disease. A feeble cry comes up occasionally from isolated stock associations, protesting against the free or virtually free importation of cattle, but this has done and will do no good. The united demand of every stock-grower in the United States will compel Congress to take action and it is doubtful if anything short of this will. Why can't stockmen see that "in union there is strength." and that by united action they can compel recognition for their just claims.
articles.summary: There is no business on the face of the earth which depends so entiely on providence and honest neighbors as the cattle business.

articles.headline: Alfalfa in Western Kansas.
articles.text: The experiment of growing alfalfa or California clover in the western portion of this State by our farmers and stockmen, has met with most flattering results. They have met with such excellent success that others are induced to seed down large tracts of land with this valuable hay and feed-producing range plant. The seeding may be done in early fall and about 30 pounds of seed should be used to the acre, which would insure a thick stand for the first season. The yield of alfalfa is enormous, as much as eight or ten tons per acre, which on good soil, such as will produce corn, can be cut four times a year. If cut for hay it should be cut just before it turns to seed or while in bloom. It may be cut twice for hay each year and the third time for seed. Alfalfa may be grazed until late in the fall and winter, then again in the spring and still make a fair seed crop. The roots of this plant go down into the soil to a depth of ten or fifteen feet, and in some instances have been known to go even deeper, to a depth where, as a rule, it would strike water. We would advise all who can to put in a field of alfalfa.—[Dodge City, Kan., Globe.
articles.summary: The experiment of growing alfalfa or California clover in the western portion of this State by our farmers and stockmen, has met with most flattering results.

articles.headline: Legislation for Grazing Region.
articles.text:
It is to be hoped that Congress will before long become sufficiently intelligent in regard to the public land system and the condition of life and business in the far west to see that some legislation is urgently needed concerning the ownership and occupancy of land in the great central grazing zone, where agriculture is not feasible, and where the only value of the soil is its capacity of furnishing pasture to stock. The existing land laws, adopted when Illinois was the remote west, have little applicability to Montana or Wyoming. Only very limited areas of the Territories can ever be occupied under the homestead and preemption acts, for the reason that not one acre in a hundred is good for farming, and those acts contemplate settlement by farmers only. The stockman is not considered at all. He can do nothing with the 320 acres which is all that he can get title to under the statutes now in force. That amount of land would not pasture enough cattle to support a family a single month. It takes about thirty acres to feed a steer the year round. What would the stockman do with ten or a dozen animals as his only resource to make a living? He cannot farm because the rainfall is not sufficient to raise crops. He must have more cattle, or more sheep, and to subsist on them he must use land that belongs to the government.

Now if the government gives farming land in the rich prairie regions to the settler who will homestead it, handing over a patent to 160 acres, and selling 160 more for $1.25 to $2.50 per acre, why should it not make some equally just and liberal provision for the settler in regions where the land is worth nothing except for grazing and not more than 25 to 50 cents an acre for that use? The settler asks no more than land enough to support his family as comfortably and with as much labor as will a quarter section in the agricultural regions. He is willing to buy this land, but the government will not sell it. The government, by virtue of its present stupid land system, makes the stockman a sort of Bedouin, for it refuses to give him the ownership of a fixed abode where he can make a living for his family.

The cattle king, with his vast herds, does not complain of the present system, for he takes posession of as much land as he needs, turns his stock upon it and employs his cowboys to look after it. The small stockman who has only a few hundred head cannot put his little band of cattle out on the public range, for in a few months they would be scattered far and wide among the herds of many different owners. He cannot afford to go to all the different round-ups and identify his animals. What we want is the right either by purchase or rental from the government to fence land enough for all his needs so that his cattle can be kept at home. What is greatly needed for the prosperity of the entire grazing belt is an expansion of the present homestead and preemption laws to adapt them to regions essentially unfit for farming. The new legislation might provide that in such regions a homestead should consist of four sections (2,560 acres), with the right of preemption and purchasing as much more. This would give permanence to the stock industry and would make it to the interest of the herdsmen to preserve the grass on the great natural pastures.—[The Northwest.

articles.headline: Citizens' Nominating Convention.
articles.text:
Citizens' Nominating Convention.

The meeting was called to order by Wm. Dantz, who nominated J. C. Fisher for chairman. Carried.

Gregor Lang was nominated and elected secretary.

The chairman stated the object of the meeting and declared nominations for county offices to be in order.

Howard Eaton nominated D. C. Rowe as commissioner from precinct No. 1. Carried unanimously.

Willis Eaton nominated J. W. Goodall as commissioner from precinct No. 2. Carried unanimously.

Fred Willard nominated J. L. Truscott as commissioner for precinct No. 3. Carried unanimously.

Dan. McKenzie nominated J. C. Williamson for county clerk and register of deeds. Carried unanimously.

Wm. Jones nominated Willis Eaton for assessor. Carried unanimously.

Willis Eaton nominated A. T. Packard for Probate Judge. He withdrew in favor of B. F. Lamb, who was nominated unanimously.

Willis Eaton nominated W. F. Van Driesche for treasurer. Carried unanimously.

J. W. Goodall nominated T. Martin for coroner. Carried unanimously.

Willis Eaton nominated Wm. Dantz for superintendent of public instruction. Carried unanimously.

Dan. McKenzie nominated F. A. Willard for sheriff. Carried unanimously.

G. G. Bond, A. T. Packard, C. F. Ellison and Howard Eaton were nominated by acclamation as justices of the peace.

Peter Pelissier, Wm. Jones, Samuel Whitney and Chas. Uderman were nominated by acclamation as constables.

On motion of Willis Eaton, Medora was named as county seat.

Adjourned.
articles.summary: Minutes of the citizens' convention that unanimously nominated the Billings County ticket and named Medora as county seat.
